questions.title: What is the distinction between 'intrinsic' evidence and Rule 404(b) 'other acts' evidence in felon-in-possession cases?
questions.question_body: In *United States v. Cutbank*, the defendant argued that testimony about him possessing the gun on previous occasions was improper propensity evidence under FRE 404(b). However, the Eighth Circuit ruled this was 'intrinsic' evidence. I am confused about the legal test for this distinction. Why does prior possession of the *same* weapon automatically become intrinsic to the charge of possession, rather than being treated as character evidence showing he is the type of person who owns guns? How does the court define the boundary where prior acts stop being part of the story and start being impermissible propensity proof?

questions.title: Does admitting an out-of-court statement for 'context' violate the Confrontation Clause if the declarant later testifies?
questions.question_body: The appellant argued that the jury shouldn't hear D.F.'s initial statements to police until she testified, to avoid hearsay and Confrontation Clause issues. The court said no limiting instruction was needed because D.F. eventually testified in person. My understanding was that the Confrontation Clause generally bars testimonial hearsay unless there is a chance for cross-examination. If the police testified about what D.F. told them *before* she took the stand, wasn't that technically using her out-of-court statement substantively without immediate cross-examination? Does the Eighth Circuit allow prosecutors to introduce these statements freely as long as the witness shows up eventually, regardless of when they testify?

questions.title: How does FRE 613 interact with authentication requirements when impeaching a witness with a police report they didn't write?
questions.question_body: During cross-examination of witness C.F., defense counsel tried to read from a police report containing C.F.'s prior inconsistent statements. The court stopped this because C.F. didn't author the report. I thought FRE 613 allowed extrinsic evidence of prior inconsistent statements to impeach a witness. Why did the court require 'authentication' of the report itself? Is there a difference between using a document to refresh recollection versus introducing it as extrinsic evidence of inconsistency, and why did the fact that a third party (the officer) wrote down C.F.'s words matter so much here?

questions.title: Can a § 3553(a) 'not greater than necessary' argument overcome a within-Guidelines sentence when ACCA mandates a high minimum?
questions.question_body: Cutbank argued that applying the § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) enhancement resulted in a sentence conflicting with 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a) because it was 'greater than necessary,' even though it fell within the Guidelines range. The court affirmed simply because the sentence was within-range and the judge considered the factors. Since the Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA) already forces a 15-year minimum based on his priors, isn't almost any within-Guidelines sentence going to be harsh? What specific factual showing does a defendant need to make to convince an appellate court that a within-Guidelines sentence is substantively unreasonable under § 3553(a), especially when statutory mandatory minimums are driving the baseline?

questions.title: Why did the court reject the argument that mentioning the victim's sister's death was unfairly prejudicial under FRE 403?
questions.question_body: When D.F. explained why her memory of guns was fuzzy, she mentioned her sister was killed by a gun. The defense moved to strike this as unfairly prejudicial emotional testimony. The court denied it, citing FRE 403 and noting it responded to cross-examination about inconsistencies. I struggle with how courts balance probative value against unfair prejudice here. Doesn't mentioning a family murder inherently inflame the jury against the defendant more than it explains memory loss? At what point does an explanation for poor recollection become too emotionally charged to be admissible?

questions.title: How does the 'harmless error' standard apply cumulatively to multiple evidentiary rulings in a criminal trial?
questions.question_body: The opinion lists several contested evidentiary rulings (prior possession testimony, timing of victim statements, impeachment limits, etc.) but ultimately affirms because any potential errors were 'harmless' given the overwhelming evidence. The court cites *DeMarce* saying reversal only happens if the jury was 'substantially swayed.' How do appellate courts analyze whether multiple small errors add up to substantial prejudice? If there were indeed five questionable rulings, doesn't their combined effect create more doubt than looking at them individually as harmless? What is the threshold for 'cumulative error' in the Eighth Circuit?
